title: Nonclustered Columnstore for Analytics
description: A rowstore GROUP BY scans in row mode; a nonclustered columnstore index enables batch-mode aggregation while the table still serves OLTP.
narrative:
## Scenario
The `Orders` table is a classic OLTP rowstore (clustered on `OrderId`). A reporting screen runs an analytical roll-up over all 500,000 rows:

```sql
SELECT Status, COUNT(*), SUM(Total) FROM Orders GROUP BY Status;
```

It does a full **Clustered Index Scan** plus a Hash Aggregate every time.

## Why it's slow
Rowstore stores whole rows together, so an aggregate over two columns still drags **every page of every row** through memory. That's fine for OLTP point lookups but wasteful for column-wide analytics.

## The fix: a nonclustered columnstore index (NCCI)
```sql
CREATE NONCLUSTERED COLUMNSTORE INDEX NCCI_Orders ON Orders(Status, Total);
```

An NCCI stores just those columns **column-by-column**, heavily compressed, and unlocks **batch-mode** execution. The optimizer now answers the GROUP BY from the columnstore — no rowstore scan — while the clustered rowstore keeps serving transactional queries. This hybrid (HTAP) pattern gives you analytics speed without a separate copy of the data.

## What to look for
- Bad: a **Clustered Index Scan** on `Orders`.
- Good: the plan reads **`NCCI_Orders`** instead (columnstore, batch mode).

> Note: columnstore scans surface in the plan as an *Index Scan* on the NCCI, and their I/O isn't counted as ordinary logical reads — so this lesson grades on the index used, not on `STATISTICS IO`.
startingQuery: SELECT Status, COUNT(*) AS Cnt, SUM(Total) AS Rev FROM Orders GROUP BY Status;
hints: The GROUP BY does a full Clustered Index Scan of the rowstore. Rowstore drags whole rows through memory even for a two-column aggregate.
A columnstore index stores columns separately, compressed, and enables batch-mode aggregation.
Add a nonclustered columnstore index: CREATE NONCLUSTERED COLUMNSTORE INDEX NCCI_Orders ON Orders(Status, Total);
